And basically, since 1965, nobody bothered to define what gainful employment was. And so for close to 50 years, nobody did anything with this phrase. But then in 2011, the Obama administration came out with the first iteration of what we now refer to as the gainful employment regulations. or just gain employment for sure. So that original version got thrown out justifiably by the court. They were focusing on a repayment rate and they didn't have very good justification for choosing the cut off that they chose. But actually the problem that I thought was even more severe with the original regulations. was it actually would have given the secretary of education veto power over any new program offered by a for-profit university. And that is just completely alien to our approach to higher education for the past 70 years, right? So the Department of Education, traditionally, and until those 2011 regulations was never allowed to basically tell us, well, no, you can't offer this type of education. And the 2011 regulations would have done that, but luckily the courts threw those out. The Obama Department of Education cleaned up those problems, issued a set of new regulations that was much more focused on kind of debt relative to earnings, which I think is a great approach, right? So two things that I really love about the 2014 edition of the game for employment regulations was number one, it was the first time that the federal government had focused on program level outcomes, which is, as I mentioned earlier, that is just a huge, huge leap in how we should be thinking about accountability and higher education. So now that we have program level data, we should only be really talking about program level accountability because it's just it's such a better way to think about accountability. A perfect example was in the original gameful employment regulations. One of the few private nonprofit programs that failed was a certificate program in theater studies or something like that at Harvard, right? Harvard's great school. Nobody would have thought anything at Harvard would fail gameful employment. And if we're looking at institution level data, nothing ever would, right? Because all the rest of Harvard's programs are doing great, presumably. We never would have known that this one program at Harvard was leading to really, really excessive debt for students who are graduating from a program. And so that I think is a perfect illustration of the value of this program level data. It avoids letting bad performing programs like good institutions, escape accountability. At the same time, it avoids punishing good programs at low performing institutions. And so program level data is really the way to go. The second thing I really liked about the gainful employment regulations, it was the first time the federal government had really taken earnings into account as an outcome of college. So something like 90% of students go to college to get a better job or to earn more money or something like pretty career focused. So college is obviously very important to achieving those goals. But until kind of gainful employment, The government, it really hadn't done anything with earnings outcomes. So that's the other thing I really liked about the gameful point regulations. And they even looked at excessive debt in a good way. So they looked at it relative to earnings. So they looked at typical debt for program students and typical earnings, which is a good way. You could quibble with the exact metrics they used or the cutoffs that they used within those metrics. One of the alternative measures that we at TPPF have introduced is something just a little easier to understand. It's just kind of total debt as a percent of annual earnings. And the reason we did that is because it's a little easier to understand. I'm just a big proponent of kind of simplicity when it comes to laws, regulations, that kind of stuff.
